claims.text: The initial Pd nanocubes are approximately 16.4–16.8 nm in size.
The initial Pd nanocubes have an FCC structure enclosed by {100} facets.
The specified precursor injection at 200°C epitaxially deposits PtRuFeCoNi shells on Pd nanocubes.
The resulting PtRuFeCoNi shell is approximately five atomic layers thick and {100}-terminated.
The shell has a square atomic arrangement with random mixing of Pt, Ru, Fe, Co, and Ni.
The randomly mixed shell exhibits local lattice distortions and orbital hybridization.
The disordered shell is kinetically stable at electrocatalytic temperatures below approximately 80°C.
Heating above approximately 300°C can cause ordering or phase separation that changes the active structure.
The multielement cocktail effect and orbital hybridization tune the hydrogen-binding free energy toward 0 eV.
Near-thermoneutral hydrogen binding produces balanced hydrogen adsorption and desorption kinetics.
Electron transfer from Fe to Ru increases Ru's hydrogen affinity during HER.
Potential-dependent OH adsorption and desorption involving Pt, Co, and Ni promotes HOR activity.
PtRuFeCoNi-coated Pd nanocubes will have higher intrinsic HER activity than commercial Pt/C and alternative IGM-PGM-HEA shells.
PtRuFeCoNi-coated Pd nanocubes will have higher intrinsic HOR activity than commercial Pt/C and alternative IGM-PGM-HEA shells.
PtRuFeCoNi-coated Pd nanocubes will lose less activity during cycling than commercial Pt/C and alternative IGM-PGM-HEA shells.
DFT predicts a median hydrogen adsorption free energy of approximately −0.01 eV for the catalyst.
The metastable randomly mixed PtRuFeCoNi shell governs HER and HOR catalytic performance.
The tuned hydrogen adsorption energetics enhance catalytic durability in addition to activity.

contradictions.description: The intervention refers to depositing 'ten quinary ... shells,' whereas the structural mediator describes a singular shell approximately five atomic layers thick. It is unclear whether 'ten' denotes ten shells, ten variants, or a shell thickness, creating an internal numerical/structural inconsistency.
